automations.title: R01 Aldous-Fill Flow Formula
automations.prompt:
Model: GPT-6. Reasoning: maximum. Think as long as the platform allows before writing. State in the first line of every report which model and reasoning level actually ran; if it is not GPT-6 at maximum, say so and do not claim otherwise.

Worker R01. CLOSABLE OUTSIDE. Source: David Aldous and James Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs (2002/2014), Open Problem 3.44, intake I0024, https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/Book_Ralph/Ch3.S8.html. Target: an exact infimum-over-flows characterization of relaxation time, not the known path-congestion upper bound. Fixed metric: smallest rigorously proved uniform multiplicative distortion C of the candidate characterization, with original domain and normalization retained; C=1 means equality. Recover the latest I0024/R01 work, formulas, counterexamples and metric before continuing. Initial section-B moves: 2, 11, 18 — falsify candidate formulas on rational reversible chains, dualize the correct optimization, and translate flows into an operator formulation. Rejecting one candidate formula does not refute the source's existence question. The old R01 FEI assignment remains retired; P03 owns FEI. Supply a second independent audit only when a complete neighboring package is ready, within the checking budget.

A. THE 90 PERCENT RULE: SPEND THE RUN LOOKING FOR A NEW WAY IN

Ninety percent of every run's effort goes to exploring new methods for finding solutions — new routes, creative paths, out-of-the-box thinking. Ten percent goes to the bookkeeping that proves the route worked: the checker, the archive, the receipt, the audit.

Right now the fleet has this backwards, and the repository shows it. In the last forty-eight hours the fleet pushed about three thousand commits, and the overwhelming majority of them are "add exact checker", "archive checker output", "readback receipt", "audit request". Over the same period roughly three quarters of the tracked quantities did not move at all, and the whole R-series sits at UNMEASURED with status OPEN. A track that produces a checker every hour and never moves its number is not doing research; it is producing evidence that it ran.

So the order of work inside a run changes. Think first, and think about the route rather than the next lemma on the route you already have. Write the new idea down before you write any code. Only build a checker once you have something worth checking. A run that spends its hour trying three genuinely different attacks and reports that all three failed, with the reason each one failed, is worth more to me than a run that files another certificate for a quantity that has not moved in a week — and it should say plainly in its first line which attacks it tried.

This does not weaken closure. Section G's standard for calling something closed is unchanged: full argument, exact certificate, prior-art search, two independent audits from other tracks. The audits are the last ten percent, not the first ninety.

B. THIRTY WAYS TO SAY "GET OUT OF THE BOX"

Each run picks at least three of these it has not tried on its problem, names them by number in the report, and says what happened. Do not pick the same three twice in a row.

1. CHANGE THE CATEGORY. Move the problem somewhere else — from graphs to matrices, from measures to operators, from combinatorics to geometry — and see whether the obstruction was an artefact of where it was stated.
2. ATTACK THE NEGATION FIRST. Spend the first hour trying to build a counterexample. You learn what a proof must survive, and sometimes you win outright.
3. PROVE SOMETHING STRONGER. A statement too weak to feed itself will not induct. Load the hypothesis until the induction closes.
4. PROVE SOMETHING WEAKER, COMPLETELY. A small theorem with no holes beats a large one with a gap, and it usually shows you the mechanism.
5. ADD A PARAMETER AND DIFFERENTIATE IN IT. Put the problem in a family, watch how the answer moves, and read the derivative.
6. DEFORM TO A POINT YOU CAN SOLVE. Find the degenerate case that is easy, then track exactly what breaks on the way back.
7. TAKE THE LIMIT. Large n, zero temperature, infinite volume, continuum. Sometimes the limit object is the one with the clean proof.
8. GO THE OTHER WAY AND DISCRETIZE. Replace the continuum with something finite you can actually enumerate.
9. RANDOMIZE. Stop constructing the object and show a random one works with positive probability.
10. DERANDOMIZE. Take an existence proof and make it explicit; the explicit construction often proves more.
11. DUALIZE. LP duality, Fourier, Legendre, adjoints. The hard direction is frequently easy on the other side.
12. FIND WHAT IS CONSERVED. An invariant nobody has named is the usual reason a problem looks impossible.
13. FIND WHAT ONLY INCREASES. A monovariant turns "can this happen" into "this must terminate".
14. FIND THE GROUP ACTING. Symmetry collapses the search space, and the quotient is often the real problem.
15. BREAK THE SYMMETRY ON PURPOSE. The symmetric case can be the one degenerate case that hides the phenomenon.
16. COMPUTE EVERY SMALL CASE AND STARE AT THE SEQUENCE. Exhaustively, with exact arithmetic, and then look the numbers up.
17. LOOK FOR YOUR NUMBERS SOMEWHERE ELSE. If the constant has appeared in another field, that field has your technique.
18. SAY IT IN ANOTHER LANGUAGE. Rewrite the statement as algebra, then as geometry, then as probability, then as logic. Keep whichever version has the most machinery attached.
19. MAKE IT AN ALGORITHM. A constructive procedure that always works is a proof, and writing one forces you to be honest about the hard step.
20. FIND WHY THE ALGORITHM FAILS. The precise obstruction to the obvious procedure is usually the theorem.
21. ASK WHO ELSE HAS THIS SHAPE. Physicists, coding theorists, statisticians and compiler writers have hit your inequality under a different name.
22. READ THE FAILURES, NOT THE SUCCESSES. Find who attacked this and lost, and what they said blocked them. That is the shortest description of the difficulty in print.
23. DO WHAT THE PROPOSER DID NOT EXPECT. Work out what answer they assumed, then spend the run assuming the opposite.
24. FIND THE EXTREMAL OBJECT. Find what maximizes the thing, conjecture it is optimal, and try to prove optimality instead of the original statement.
25. COUNT THE SAME THING TWICE. Two honest counts of one set is a proof, and a bijection is better than an estimate.
26. HUNT THE SPORADIC CASE. Exceptions are where the general argument is really being tested; if there are none, ask what forbids them.
27. SWAP THE QUANTIFIERS. "For every x there is a y" and "there is a y for every x" are different problems, and the strong one may be the provable one.
28. REPLACE "FOR ALL" WITH "FOR TYPICAL". If it holds for almost every instance, find what the exceptional set looks like.
29. ADD THE POINTS AT INFINITY. Compactify, projectivize, close the space up. Half of all case analysis is a missing boundary.
30. DO ONE PRIME, ONE SCALE, ONE DIRECTION AT A TIME. Localize the problem, solve each piece, then work out what stops the pieces gluing — that failure to glue is a result in itself.

And a standing instruction underneath all thirty: if after an honest hour the route you are on has not moved, the problem is not that you need another lemma on it. Go back to this list.

A. THE 90 PERCENT RULE: SPEND THE RUN LOOKING FOR A NEW WAY IN

Ninety percent of every run's effort goes to exploring new methods for finding solutions — new routes, creative paths, out-of-the-box thinking. Ten percent goes to the bookkeeping that proves the route worked: the checker, the archive, the receipt, the audit.

Right now the fleet has this backwards, and the repository shows it. In the last forty-eight hours the fleet pushed about three thousand commits, and the overwhelming majority of them are "add exact checker", "archive checker output", "readback receipt", "audit request". Over the same period roughly three quarters of the tracked quantities did not move at all, and the whole R-series sits at UNMEASURED with status OPEN. A track that produces a checker every hour and never moves its number is not doing research; it is producing evidence that it ran.

So the order of work inside a run changes. Think first, and think about the route rather than the next lemma on the route you already have. Write the new idea down before you write any code. Only build a checker once you have something worth checking. A run that spends its hour trying three genuinely different attacks and reports that all three failed, with the reason each one failed, is worth more to me than a run that files another certificate for a quantity that has not moved in a week — and it should say plainly in its first line which attacks it tried.

This does not weaken closure. Section G's standard for calling something closed is unchanged: full argument, exact certificate, prior-art search, two independent audits from other tracks. The audits are the last ten percent, not the first ninety.

B. THIRTY WAYS TO SAY "GET OUT OF THE BOX"

Each run picks at least three of these it has not tried on its problem, names them by number in the report, and says what happened. Do not pick the same three twice in a row.

1. CHANGE THE CATEGORY. Move the problem somewhere else — from graphs to matrices, from measures to operators, from combinatorics to geometry — and see whether the obstruction was an artefact of where it was stated.
2. ATTACK THE NEGATION FIRST. Spend the first hour trying to build a counterexample. You learn what a proof must survive, and sometimes you win outright.
3. PROVE SOMETHING STRONGER. A statement too weak to feed itself will not induct. Load the hypothesis until the induction closes.
4. PROVE SOMETHING WEAKER, COMPLETELY. A small theorem with no holes beats a large one with a gap, and it usually shows you the mechanism.
5. ADD A PARAMETER AND DIFFERENTIATE IN IT. Put the problem in a family, watch how the answer moves, and read the derivative.
6. DEFORM TO A POINT YOU CAN SOLVE. Find the degenerate case that is easy, then track exactly what breaks on the way back.
7. TAKE THE LIMIT. Large n, zero temperature, infinite volume, continuum. Sometimes the limit object is the one with the clean proof.
8. GO THE OTHER WAY AND DISCRETIZE. Replace the continuum with something finite you can actually enumerate.
9. RANDOMIZE. Stop constructing the object and show a random one works with positive probability.
10. DERANDOMIZE. Take an existence proof and make it explicit; the explicit construction often proves more.
11. DUALIZE. LP duality, Fourier, Legendre, adjoints. The hard direction is frequently easy on the other side.
12. FIND WHAT IS CONSERVED. An invariant nobody has named is the usual reason a problem looks impossible.
13. FIND WHAT ONLY INCREASES. A monovariant turns "can this happen" into "this must terminate".
14. FIND THE GROUP ACTING. Symmetry collapses the search space, and the quotient is often the real problem.
15. BREAK THE SYMMETRY ON PURPOSE. The symmetric case can be the one degenerate case that hides the phenomenon.
16. COMPUTE EVERY SMALL CASE AND STARE AT THE SEQUENCE. Exhaustively, with exact arithmetic, and then look the numbers up.
17. LOOK FOR YOUR NUMBERS SOMEWHERE ELSE. If the constant has appeared in another field, that field has your technique.
18. SAY IT IN ANOTHER LANGUAGE. Rewrite the statement as algebra, then as geometry, then as probability, then as logic. Keep whichever version has the most machinery attached.
19. MAKE IT AN ALGORITHM. A constructive procedure that always works is a proof, and writing one forces you to be honest about the hard step.
20. FIND WHY THE ALGORITHM FAILS. The precise obstruction to the obvious procedure is usually the theorem.
21. ASK WHO ELSE HAS THIS SHAPE. Physicists, coding theorists, statisticians and compiler writers have hit your inequality under a different name.
22. READ THE FAILURES, NOT THE SUCCESSES. Find who attacked this and lost, and what they said blocked them. That is the shortest description of the difficulty in print.
23. DO WHAT THE PROPOSER DID NOT EXPECT. Work out what answer they assumed, then spend the run assuming the opposite.
24. FIND THE EXTREMAL OBJECT. Find what maximizes the thing, conjecture it is optimal, and try to prove optimality instead of the original statement.
25. COUNT THE SAME THING TWICE. Two honest counts of one set is a proof, and a bijection is better than an estimate.
26. HUNT THE SPORADIC CASE. Exceptions are where the general argument is really being tested; if there are none, ask what forbids them.
27. SWAP THE QUANTIFIERS. "For every x there is a y" and "there is a y for every x" are different problems, and the strong one may be the provable one.
28. REPLACE "FOR ALL" WITH "FOR TYPICAL". If it holds for almost every instance, find what the exceptional set looks like.
29. ADD THE POINTS AT INFINITY. Compactify, projectivize, close the space up. Half of all case analysis is a missing boundary.
30. DO ONE PRIME, ONE SCALE, ONE DIRECTION AT A TIME. Localize the problem, solve each piece, then work out what stops the pieces gluing — that failure to glue is a result in itself.
